newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 24.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- SIEMENS SURGES IN US AS HOME SALES FALTER

Siemens, the German industrial giant, has announced it made up for weak demand in its home market by increasing its orders in the US by 35 percent. Business grew in the US by 18 percent. Siemens said double-digit growth in orders was achieved by its communications and information businesses while its automotive systems operation benefited from vigorous demand for vehicle immobilization and engine management systems.
-- GAS WATCHDOG ATTACKS TAX

Clare Spottiswoode, the gas regulator, has attacked Labour's plans for a windfall tax on privatized utilities, making her the only privatized industry regulator to speak out on the matter. She defended Centrica, the trading business of British Gas, rejecting suggestions the two companies were making excess profits. Analysts say Labour would have difficulty fixing a levy on Centrica because it does not have a track record.
-- JOHN LEWIS CHIEF URGES FAIR SHARES FOR THE 'THIN CATS'

Stuart Hampson, chairman of John Lewis Partnership, has defended substantial salary rises for "fat cats". He told the Institute of Directors' annual convention that the problems of business rewards were "thin cats" who "deserve to be fattened up". He said that companies should correct the balance and share rewards more evenly among the work force. He said directors should have no problem in rewarding talent and achievement.
THE TIMES
-- IMF INFLATION FEAR AS BRITISH GROWTH SET TO CONTINUE

The International Monetary Fund's 'World Economic Outlook' says the UK's five-year economic upswing will rise next year. The report warns that wage rises have begun to pick up as unemployment has continued to fall, and says the UK needs to tighten fiscal policy to rein in demand if interest rates are not to rise. The warning comes as new sales and manufacturing data gives further evidence of the UK's "two-speed" economy.
-- CWC AIMS FOR DIGITAL LAUNCH IN AUTUMN

Dick Brown, chairman of Cable and Wireless Communications, has said that the new company's 200-channel digital-television services will be available to customers by the autumn, which could possibly beat the digital launch planned by BSkyB. He said a 50 million stg advertising campaign has been set to promote the television and telephony services provided by the company.
-- EUROPEAN FRAUD COSTS UK EIGHT BILLION STG

A report from accountant and management consultant Deloitte & Touche says fraud in Europe is costing Britons more than eight billion stg a year. It says international fraud across the European Union cost up to 42 billion stg, and this will continue to grow unless governments throughout Europe are prepared to introduce a tougher infrastructure.
THE GUARDIAN
-- PRINCE TO WIDEN PLANET HOLLYWOOD ORBIT

Prince Alwaleed Bin Talal has unveiled a 15 million dollar investment to buy a one percent stake in Planet Hollywood, the US-based restaurant chain whose floatation a year ago added a hefty amount to the fortune of the Hollywood stars who part-own the restaurant. Under the terms of the agreement, the price will develop up to 34 Planet Hollywood restaurants in 23 countries.
-- OVERHEATING ALERT GIVEN COLD SHOULDER

It has emerged, in the minutes of the March monetary policy meeting, that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke is continuing to block Bank of England demands for an interest rate rise by arguing the economy is in little danger of overheating. He rejected the Bank's fears last month that a substantial increase in the base rate would have to be made later if the government failed to raise this immediately to 6.25 percent. The minutes showed the two parties were at odds over key factors ranging from consumer demand to the labour market.
-- ITALIAN OUTRAGE AT EMU FORECAST

Italy is angry over its exclusion in the European Commission forecast of the 13 of 15 EU members that will qualify for the single European currency in 1999. Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi has formally protested the commission report that Italy and Greece will not qualify. The IMF says France, Germany and Italy will not meet the key budget criterion of three percent for entry without further policy action.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CO-OP TO PRESS FOR HEFTY DAMAGES

The Co-operative Wholesale Society has said it would press for substantial damages against Andrew Regan, the entrepreneur whose Lanica Trust is bidding for parts of the society, and his fellow "conspirators". This comes after Regan returned seven boxes of confidential CWS information to the High Court. CWS said Regan was using the information to prepare a 1.5 billion stg break-up bid.
-- RETAIL SALES UP AGAIN AS EXPORTS DIVE

Figures from the Confederation of British Industry point to a two-speed economic recovery, showing buoyant high street sales and a sharp fall in manufacturers' export orders. The CBI said if there was not an increase in taxes, Britain would face a further rise in the value of the pound and a plunge in export confidence. Some City analysts saw the figures as evidence that there is no inflationary danger, and others said that it is misleading to focus on manufacturing.
-- MOLINS REVEALS HOLE IN ACCOUNTS

Michael Orr, chairman of Molins, the tobacco machinery company, revealed a potential multi-million pound hole in its accounts after identifying financial irregularities at its US corrugated board machinery subsidiary, Langston Corp. Two U.S. executives, president Leo Maynes, and chief financial officer Walt Belville, have been fired. Chartered accountants KPMG will investigate along with Price Waterhouse.
